new.title: Spacetime contactability in Galactic civilization networks: Contact counts and percolation
new.summary: The number of Galactic civilizations does not determine whether they are in contact. Allowing civilizations to appear at different times separates listening, audibility, mutual-listening, and relay networks, with a distinct reply-closing condition requiring a return signal within the sender's lifetime. For each network we derive the contact counts and estimate the connectivity threshold in a uniform population, then apply the results to a structured Galactic disc, separating the detection range $d_{\rm max}$ from the light horizon $cL$ through $\chi=d_{\rm max}/cL$. The contactability is $\eta=\pi n d_{\rm max}^{2}$, where $n$ is the active civilization surface density. Averaged over civilization appearances, the lifetime listening count is $2\eta$ for all $\chi$ and, at fixed detection range, for any lifetime distribution. Audibility and mutual-listening counts sum to $4\eta$, but connectivity depends on threshold behavior rather than counts alone. As $\chi\rightarrow0$, the listening threshold decreases from the coeval value $4.51$ to $1.32\pm0.01$. Assuming an ideal complete survey, our own non-detection gives the reference bound $\eta(R_0)\le2.75$ at the Sun's Galactocentric radius. This benchmark lies above the listening, audibility and relay thresholds throughout the range studied. Unlike the coeval model, the spacetime model can satisfy both this benchmark and a local connectivity criterion, moving the local-contact frontier outward by $3.2$ kpc. Under the same benchmark, civilizations hear at most $5.5$ others on average, while the mean reply-closing count falls below unity for $\chi\gtrsim1$. Contact may therefore be common even when completed replies remain rare.

new.title: Mitigating oscillatory systematics in MeerKLASS L-band H i intensity maps
new.summary: HI intensity mapping is a promising probe of the large-scale structure of the Universe, but is limited by foregrounds and instrumental systematics. For the MeerKAT Large Area Synoptic Survey (MeerKLASS) L-band data, it is found that emission line stacking measurement reveals a type of systematics related to the instrument beam. Using simulations with a full-sky electromagnetic beam model, we show that the chromaticity and sidelobes of the MeerKAT beam modulate the frequency-smooth foreground emission and introduce oscillating structures that persist after foreground removal. The beam rotates with respect to the sky between two types of scans, and combining datasets with different beam orientations before foreground cleaning makes the residuals stronger. In MeerKLASS L-band data, processing these two types of scans separately significantly suppresses the oscillating residuals while preserving the stacked HI signal. The ratio of the HI signal amplitude to the systematic fluctuation amplitude increases by 81%. We find an oscillating structure in PCA mode 11 in our previous data processing, but simply removing this mode does not improve the stacked spectrum due to the signal loss. Our strategy can help mitigate spectral ripples that are induced by the beam in future MeerKAT and SKA-Mid surveys.

new.title: Aster: A Flexible and Robust Collection of Numerical Tools for N-Body Problems
new.summary: The Aster library is an open-source collection of numerical tools designed for large-scale gravitational N-body simulations. Aster provides a flexible environment to its users, enabling it to be used in the analysis of a broad range of astrophysical problems. The library implements efficient force calculation algorithms, including a spatial tree solver optimized with coordinate-dependent identifiers, which has been fine-tuned for both CPU and GPU architectures. Despite its high degree of modularity, many parts of the library have been optimized with SIMD instructions, heavy parallelization, and support on dedicated hardware. Aster also offers a wide variety of numerical symplectic integrators, such as SABA (from first to tenth order), the classic leapfrog algorithm, and the more advanced Wisdom-Holman (WH) integrator, while also providing a vast collection of mathematical tools, e.g., post-newtonian expansions (1PN, 2PN, 2.5PN), data collection and graphing systems, a built-in renderer, and presets for faster instantiation of large amounts of bodies. In this work we will discuss in depth the details of each module as well as the results of several performance- and accuracy-related tests, probing the library's capabilities in different physical applications.

new.title: Mars Seed: A Reference Architecture for Biomanufacturing Habitats from Martian Resources
new.summary: Human exploration of Mars will require enormous quantities of materials for the first crewed missions and substantially more for permanent habitation, making flexible and scalable technologies for in situ resource utilization (ISRU), including biological ISRU, of significant interest. However, no existing mission architecture quantitatively evaluates whether in situ biomanufacturing can realistically deliver materials at the scales required for human settlement. Here, we present Mars Seed, an end-to-end reference architecture for using biomanufacturing to produce bioplastics at scale entirely from in situ resources on Mars. We provide a complete analysis of a space bioprocess in which feedstocks are generated entirely from Martian resources, converted biologically into polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB) bioplastic, and purified to produce material suitable for constructing human habitats. We show that the upfront power and upmass costs of deploying the equipment required for this bioprocess are recovered within two synodic periods relative to Earth-shipped alternatives. Further, because the process relies entirely on feedstocks sourced from Martian materials, production can continue until equipment failure without requiring additional materials from Earth, enabling scalable conversion of local resources into useful materials. Mars Seed demonstrates that biological ISRU can be mass- and power-competitive with Earth-shipped alternatives, establishing biomanufacturing as a practical component of Mars mission architecture rather than an aspirational capability.

new.title: STarlight Acquisition and Reflection toward Interferometry (STARI) mission
new.summary: We introduce the NASA-funded mission STARI (STarlight Acquisition and Reflection toward Interferometry), a two-spacecraft technology demonstrator for future long-baseline interferometers. STARI will perform, to our knowledge, the first in-space transfer of starlight between free-flying spacecraft, a critical step toward long-baseline space interferometry. Two propulsive 8U CubeSats in low Earth orbit will fly in formation with separations up to 200 m: one relays a narrow stellar beam to the other, where an off-axis parabola reimages it into a single-mode fiber. Using differential GNSS, visible LED beacons, and fast-steering mirrors in closed-loop control, we aim to sustain diffraction-limited, high-throughput fiber coupling during formation flight. STARI, targeting launch in 2029, is designed to mature key technologies needed for future mission concepts such as the Large Interferometer for Exoplanets (LIFE), which would seek atmospheric biomarkers on nearby Earth-like exoplanets.

new.title: Extracting Published Discussions of 13,616 Galaxies with Language Models
new.summary: Astronomers often have difficulty determining whether an object, such as a star or galaxy of interest, has been discussed in the literature. Existing tools enable object identification and linking in papers but do not record whether an object was genuinely discussed in a paper or just appears in a table or catalog. We address this by using language model agents to identify galaxies discussed in more than two sentences across a corpus of 156,006 arXiv astro-ph papers and extract those discussions. We extract 44,332 discussions of individual galaxies containing 85,314 quotes from 18,641 papers. With sky coordinates for 98.2% of discussions, we group them into 13,616 galaxies. We bring these results together into GalaxyWiki, where users can find literature discussing galaxies, read what was said about them, and follow links to the source papers. new.title: Beyond the Fast Rotators: A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury Survey of Substellar Weather
new.summary: Atmospheric variability provides a unique window into the three-dimensional structure, dynamics, and evolution of brown dwarf and giant exoplanet atmospheres. Recent JWST time-resolved spectroscopic observations have revealed complex wavelength-dependent variability, offering unprecedented insights into cloud structures, thermal perturbations, and atmospheric chemistry. However, existing programs have focused primarily on individual benchmarks and specific scientific questions, resulting in heterogeneous spectral and temporal coverage and leaving important regions of the substellar population underexplored, particularly across a broad range of rotation periods, spectral types, and viewing geometries. A JWST Multi-Cycle Treasury program could systematically investigate substellar weather across a diverse, well-characterized population. By combining broad infrared spectroscopic coverage with observations spanning multiple rotations and strategically selected epochs, this program would constrain the contributions of different physical mechanisms while investigating how atmospheric structures depend on rotation, viewing geometry, and fundamental physical properties. Extended monitoring would also improve rotational-period determinations and reveal how atmospheric features evolve from rotation to rotation and over longer timescales. This coordinated effort would provide a consistently designed and uniformly processed dataset of time-resolved spectra and variability diagnostics, enabling population-level comparisons, testing predictions from three-dimensional circulation models, and establishing a framework for interpreting the atmospheric diversity and evolution of brown dwarfs and directly imaged giant exoplanets.

new.title: ExoPlanetLab: Bayesian orbit fitting of Gaia-DR4 epoch astrometry, radial velocities and relative astrometry
new.summary: Gaia Data Release 4 (DR4) provides epoch astrometry from which thousands of giant planets and many substellar and stellar companions can be characterised. We present ExoPlanetLab, an open-source package for Bayesian orbit inference from Gaia epoch astrometry, radial velocities (RVs) and relative astrometry, validated on simulated and real data. The model orbit is compared with the epoch residuals after removing the part absorbed by the single-star fit. A Student-t likelihood describes heavy-tailed data. A robust Keplerian periodogram with bootstrap false-alarm probabilities gives starting values for a joint fit. Five samplers are available: tempered ensemble MCMC, two nested samplers and two reversible-jump samplers. Evidences for a fixed number of companions select that number. Acceleration and scan-angle models test whether an orbit is warranted. The samplers agree within 0.1 sigma on a simulated two-planet system. In 180 injections all fits converge, and all signals with signal-to-noise ratio S >= 10 are detected. The posteriors show no significant bias, but the period coverage is below nominal: 90% of the true periods lie within their 95% credible intervals. None of 30 companion-free data sets gives a false detection. On DR4 pre-release data the orbit of Gaia BH3 is recovered within 1.4 sigma of published solutions. The Student-t model brings the astrometric period and eccentricity of HD 114762 onto its RV orbit. Eight simulated relative positions narrow the period's credible interval to 0.27 of its width, and Octofitter agrees within 0.2 sigma on the same data. The code is validated for single sources with DR4-like epoch astrometry, with or without RVs. Relative astrometry is tested on simulated data only. The main limits are an uncorrelated noise model and the computing cost, which grows linearly with the number of measurements and steeply with the number of companions.

new.title: DustER: Dust Extinction with Photometric Red Galaxies
new.summary: We present DustER, a new method for reconstructing dust reddening maps from photometric galaxy survey data. DustER uses red galaxies as "standard crayons". That is, it relies on the mean color of red-sequence galaxies being independent of their position in the sky. Given the galaxy's redshift, the difference between a galaxy's observed color and its expected color measures the reddening by dust along the galaxy's line of sight. When using photometric galaxy survey data, the method must rely on photometric redshifts, which, combined with selection effects, bias the recovered dust maps. DustER uses a novel approach to characterize and correct for these biases by leveraging the known statistical properties of the distribution of dust around the Milky Way. Testing on simulations, we find that the recovered dust maps are contaminated by large-scale structure. However, when we use the DustER map to deredden and select red-sequence galaxies, we find the resulting two-point function is not contaminated by dust.

new.title: SHINE: Shear inference environment - Generative forward modelling for radio weak gravitational lensing
new.summary: Next-generation radio interferometers, such as SKA, will observe the radio sky with unprecedented sensitivity and resolution enabling weak gravitational lensing studies using radio data, which not only complement optical observations but also probe higher redshifts. However, traditional shear estimation methods, based on measuring the ellipticity of observed galaxies, are not directly applicable to radio interferometric data. Interferometric observations are acquired in the Fourier domain, where galaxy images are delocalised, making shape measurements non-trivial. Furthermore, deconvolution methods such as CLEAN can introduce systematic errors when converting observations to the image domain, biasing shear estimates. To address these challenges, we propose a cosmic shear inference method based on forward generative modelling, which avoids explicit shape measurements. Our forward model simulates galaxy images, applies the shear transformation and, by including the instrumental response of the radio interferometer, simulates the visibilities of observed galaxies, with the likelihood explicitly defined in Fourier space. Using Monte Carlo sampling algorithms, we estimate the posterior distribution of the cosmic shear conditioned on a set of galaxy observations that share a common shear. We obtain unbiased shear estimates with sub-percent accuracy when applied to parametric galaxy simulations. We compare our method to state-of-the-art shear estimators, demonstrating a reduction in uncertainty of up to 3 times and no apparent multiplicative bias. We then show that applying this parametric model to COSMOS galaxies with realistic morphologies introduces a bias in the shear estimate over 10{\sigma}. Finally, we demonstrate that, by incorporating a generative forward model based on an autoencoder architecture trained on real galaxy images, we can mitigate this bias to below the 2{\sigma} level.

new.title: Learning a model of non-stationary nuisances with non-local correlations for object detection
new.summary: We tackle the problem of detecting faint objects in multivariate data corrupted by a strong and spatially correlated nuisance component in the low-sample regime. Standard covariance-based models often yield unstable or ill-conditioned estimators of the nuisance statistics, severely degrading detection performance. We propose a data-driven approach based on sparse precision matrix modeling, where the precision matrix is approximated through a pivoted sparse Cholesky factorization whose non-zeros coefficients are learned by maximum likelihood. This yields a low-complexity yet expressive statistical model of the nuisance. Building on this model, we derive a generalized likelihood ratio test for faint source detection enabling direct control of the false alarm rate. The approach is evaluated on an astrophysical application: the detection of exoplanets by high contrast imaging, where it achieves state-of-the-art performance.

cross.title: EoSAlign: An Open-Source Software for Calculating, Comparing, and Aligning Pressure Under Extreme Conditions
cross.summary: Accurate pressure determination is essential in high pressure experiments. Inconsistencies among pressure scales limit direct comparisons and contribute to uncertainty in measured properties, such as, phase boundaries, melting conditions, and thermodynamic models, especially above 100 GPa where existing scales diverge by >10 GPa. EoSAlign, an open-source software, can calculate, compare, and align pressures using a range of published calibrations. EoSAlign calculates pressure from experimental measurements (such as volume (A^3), Raman shift (cm^-1), or luminescence peak position (nm)) and it can be used to compare pressure values from different pressure standards. Using EoSAlign, we fit and align the bridgmanite and post-perovskite equations of state to a common scale, enabling us to reduce pressure scale related differences. EoSAlign can be applied to any high pressure data analysis to compare experimental results, improve consistency between studies, and advance our understanding of planetary interiors and high pressure physics.

cross.title: Leveraging Large Language Models to Predict Atomic Oxygen Erosion of Polymers in Low Earth Orbit
cross.summary: Low Earth orbit (LEO), home to most active satellites, is projected to undergo a debris-fragmentation cascade known as Kessler Syndrome. In light of this eventuality, it is imperative to maximize the operational lifetime of LEO satellites. Instrumental to this goal is the development of next-generation polymeric materials with improved resistance to atomic oxygen (AO) erosion. Because genuine LEO exposure experiments are prohibitively expensive and LEO conditions are difficult to reproduce in the laboratory, data-driven approaches offer a promising alternative for accelerating materials discovery. Here, we develop a fine-tuned large language model (LLM) based on OpenAI's GPT-4o to predict the AO erosion yield ($E_y$) of polymers using a curated dataset of 201 measurements compiled from multiple NASA LEO exposure missions. The model achieves an order of magnitude error (OME) of 0.154 and a log-scaled coefficient of determination (log-$R^2$) of 0.719, outperforming conventional machine learning approaches while eliminating the need for extensive feature engineering. Notably, incorporating macroscopic descriptors such as film thickness and layering did not improve predictive performance, suggesting that AO erosion is governed primarily by chemical and environmental variables rather than bulk structural characteristics. This finding underscores the importance of chemically informed polymer design in developing materials with improved AO resistance, while demonstrating the ability of modern LLMs to effectively extract chemically meaningful relationships even when data is limited. Beyond its predictive accuracy, the proposed framework provides a scalable platform for rapidly screening candidate polymers, reducing reliance on costly spaceflight experiments.

cross.title: First results from a borehole network for the seismic characterization of the Einstein Telescope Euregio Meuse-Rhine candidate site
cross.summary: The low-frequency sensitivity of the Einstein Telescope depends on the seismic environment of its site, both through the mechanical coupling of ground motion to the test masses and through Newtonian noise. We present the first results of the seismic characterization of the Euregio Meuse-Rhine candidate site based on a network of recently instrumented boreholes covering the first seven months of 2026 at four underground stations and their co-located surface sensors. Two of these boreholes were deliberately sited next to railway infrastructure, so that the levels reported here describe how anthropogenic transients propagate to depth at different distances from the source. The analysis was carried out with \texttt{SiteChar}, a Python framework developed for this work to provide a common processing pipeline across different sensors, networks and observation periods. It processes the data in sequential chunks and separates the noise floor from the contribution of transients. We present a characterization of the catalogue of observed transients and a tentative classification. These measurements form part of an integrated site characterization approach that combines the observed seismic field with three-dimensional geological and wave-propagation models to predict Newtonian noise and ultimately guide its mitigation at the Euregio Meuse-Rhine candidate site.

cross.title: Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit
cross.summary: Exoplanet imaging is the main method for detailed characterization of planets orbiting beyond 1 au but it requires suppressing the bright glare of the star to see the faint planet light. As well as sophisticated instrumentation, effective image processing is necessary for starlight suppression, which continues to be a substantial limitation. Standard algorithms use reference images for starlight modelling and thus they are limited by inevitable telescope instabilities that change from reference to science observation. Addressing this challenge will increase the number of planets amenable to direct imaging and will be a notable step towards imaging exo-Earths with future observatories. Here we present a new physics-based method for starlight subtraction. Our method combines a multistep optimization with a flexible physical model to produce a starlight model, allowing modelling and compensation of instrument instabilities. We use automatic differentiation (autodiff) to optimize millions of model parameters. We demonstrate our method on observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam) coronagraph instrument. We achieve sensitivity 2-15 times superior to standard techniques, including the first detection of 51 Eridani b at 4.3 $\mu$m. This is the first time, to our knowledge, that such an approach has demonstrated substantially improved sensitivity on real, on-sky coronagraphic imaging. Our framework can be extended to other current and future ground-based and space-based observatories, including the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), potentially relaxing the unprecedented stability requirements needed to make these a success.

cross.title: Millimeter-Wavelength Constraints on Circular Polarization of the Cosmic Microwave Background at Arcminute Scales with the Simons Array
cross.summary: We present constraints on the cosmic microwave background (CMB) circular polarization anisotropy at arcminute angular scales, using dedicated measurements from the Simons Array taken with a quarter-wave plate and rotating half-wave plate. A detection of circular polarization in the CMB would probe a range of proposed generation mechanisms, from Standard Model astrophysics to physics beyond it. At an observing frequency of 90 GHz, we place constraints over the multipole range $300 \leq \ell \leq 2000$, corresponding to angular scales of 5.4-36 arcmin, in bands of width $\Delta \ell = 100$, roughly tripling the highest multipole previously reached by a $V$-mode power spectrum measurement. Within this domain, we constrain the 95% confidence upper bound of $\ell (\ell+1) C_\ell^{VV} / (2\pi)$ to range from ${\sim}22\,\mu\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{CMB}^2$ at the $\ell = 350$ bandpower to ${\sim}3.5\times10^3\,\mu\mathrm{K}_\mathrm{CMB}^2$ at the $\ell = 1950$ bandpower. These limits are derived from ${\sim}2.5$ months of observations of each of two small regions of the sky located away from the Galactic plane, totaling ${\sim}12\,\mathrm{deg}^2$ of effective sky area. Because the methodology of this study marginalizes known foreground contamination, these bounds serve as robust, conservative limits on the true CMB circular polarization signal down to the sensitivity limits of the instrument. Additionally, we provide an experimental and analytical framework for implementing circular polarization observations on other telescopes by utilizing a quarter-wave plate and half-wave plate design.

cross.summary: We present experimental results from Starlink for pseudorange-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), emulating a system that fuses a primary communications mission with a secondary low-Earth orbit (LEO) PNT mission. Legacy global navigation satellite system (GNSS) constellations faceinherent vulnerabilities and signal limitations, prompting growing interest in broadband LEO constellations---such as SpaceX's Starlink---for resilient PNT. However, opportunistic use of stand-alone Starlink signals fails to achieve GNSS-competitive accuracy due to frame timing irregularities and reliance on uncorrected poor-quality publicly available ephemeris data. To overcome these limitations, we present a mock implementation of a fused LEO GNSS architecture. Our method extracts time-of-arrival observables from live Starlink Ku-band downlinks and pairs them with high-fidelity, beam-specific orbit and clock models distributed as if provided natively by the constellation operator. In a field campaign, and despite constraints imposed by consumer-grade receiver hardware, the method yields 95% error bounds of 2.33 m horizontally (semi-major axis), 3.37 m vertically, and 11.19 ns in timing, with the actual solution errors falling well within these bounds.

cross.title: Empirical constraints on cosmic-ray scattering in NGC 1333 from dust polarisation
cross.summary: Cosmic rays (CRs) regulate molecular-cloud ionization and chemistry. Gyro-resonant scattering by magnetic fluctuations sets their mean free path and, on larger scales, their effective diffusion coefficient. However, coefficients inferred from CR distributions averaged over cloud to Galactic scales leave local magnetic structure unresolved. We use the magnetic-field structure of NGC 1333 and its embedded protostellar core IRAS 4A to estimate local CR scattering rates and effective diffusion coefficients, $D(E)$, and examine their variation with environment and scale. We analyse JCMT/POL-2 maps of nine NGC 1333 regions and ALMA Band 7 maps of two IRAS 4A regions. We estimate plane-of-sky field strengths and derive fluctuation spectra from polarisation-angle structure functions. Where these spectra are sufficiently constrained, we apply quasi-linear gyro-resonant theory to calculate CR pitch-angle scattering rates and $D(E)$. The measured fluctuations constrain CR scattering over proton energy intervals of approximately 0.24-5.3 PeV in NGC 1333 and 10-57 TeV in IRAS 4A. Within these intervals, $D(E)$ spans approximately $3\times10^{28}$-$10^{31}\,{\rm cm^2\,s^{-1}}$. Scattering varies substantially between regions and is stronger where the magnetic-field angular dispersion is greater. Extrapolation to common energies suggests scattering in IRAS 4A is one to two orders of magnitude stronger than its surroundings. Within the directly probed intervals, the scattering mean free paths exceed the individual region sizes. The inferred diffusion coefficients therefore characterise local scattering conditions. A cloud-scale diffusive regime requires CRs to sample multiple regions with different scattering rates. Dust polarisation observations therefore provide constraints on CR scattering in clouds, connecting scattering to cloud-scale transport at energies accessible to $\gamma$-ray observatories.

cross.title: The PAU Survey: Dissecting strong-lensing systems with narrow-band photometric redshifts
cross.summary: Wide-field imaging surveys such as Euclid will identify large samples of strong-lens candidates, whose scientific use requires redshifts for both deflectors and lensed sources. Source redshifts are challenging because faint arcs are blended with foreground light. We test lens-model-informed photometry on eight known strong lenses, using broad-band models to define component regions, point-reflection subtraction to reduce contamination, and PAU Survey narrow bands combined with five HSC or CFHT broad bands. BCNz estimates separate lens and source redshift distributions without imposing their expected ordering. All eight lens redshift peaks agree with spectroscopy within $|\delta_z|\leq0.014$, where $\delta_z=(z_b-z_{\rm spec})/(1+z_{\rm spec})$. Four source peaks, all at $z_{\rm s}^{\rm spec}\leq1.23$, agree within $|\delta_z|\leq0.025$. Symmetric subtraction reduces the median source $|\delta_z|$ from 0.336 to 0.071. At $|\delta_z|<0.05$, narrow- plus broad-band photometry yields eight lens and four source matches, versus three and two using EAZY with broad bands alone. These results demonstrate component redshift recovery in blended systems and support redshift-based lens-candidate assessment alongside morphology and colour. Larger narrow-band surveys, including J-PAS, could extend this approach, pending uncertainty calibration and blind candidate tests.

cross.title: An Archival Search for Outer Solar System Objects in the NOIRLab Source Catalog DR2: 65 Candidates, Including Four L4 Neptune Trojans
cross.summary: I search the single-epoch detections of the NOIRLab Source Catalog DR2 (DECam, 2012-2019) for outer Solar System objects. Single-night detections are linked with a bound orbit model, vetted against artefacts, static sources and known objects, and confirmed by forced measurements on at least two new archival nights. The linker recovers 96% of known objects present on four nights in one sky tile, but end-to-end recall is about 7%, limited by cadence, tiling and catalogue incompleteness; no selection function is provided. Of 81 catalogue objects, four are designated; of the other 77, 53 are in evidence class A (multi-opposition, at least nine nights), 12 in class B and 12 in class C (not counted). On exposures never used in a fit, forced photometry detects 41 testable objects at 99% of predicted positions, as for known TNOs, against 6% at control positions; 22 pass a post hoc rule, 19 are inconclusive, none fails. Shifted controls were never confirmed by the archival image search (0 of 11,467) but were in 2.2% of trials by the catalogue precovery behind most scripted confirmations, so its nights alone are not sufficient. For the 65 class A and B candidates, 10-Myr integrations give four candidate L4 Neptune Trojans with 13-19 yr arcs, 21 resonant, 13 detached, nine scattering, two Centaurs and 16 classical objects; a detached class-B candidate has q=48.8 au. No object beyond 80 au was confirmed, which barely constrains Planet Nine. Positions are withheld until designation or 2027 June 30; their digests are published.

cross.title: New Constraints on the Ultrahigh Energy Neutrino Flux from the First Array-Wide Search with the Askaryan Radio Array
cross.summary: Ultrahigh energy neutrinos ($E_\nu \gtrsim 100$ PeV) are detectable through Askaryan emission---the nanosecond-scale radio impulse emitted by relativistic particle cascades in a dielectric medium. The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA), an Askaryan detector array located at the South Pole, has been taking data for more than a decade. We present the first array-wide search for diffuse ultrahigh energy neutrinos with ARA. The search found no events on an expected background of $0.13\pm0.01\text{ (stat.)}^{+0.05}_{-0.06}\text{ (syst.)}$ events. The resulting upper limit is the most stringent from $50$ EeV to $1000$ EeV and provides the first constraints on the flux reported by the KM3NeT Collaboration that are complementary to optical Cherenkov and particle detectors. This limit also constrains UHECR source models, and excludes some models with trans-GZK proton populations at the $90\%$ confidence level. This represents the largest Askaryan detector dataset ever analyzed, demonstrating the feasibility and sensitivity of searches with large detector arrays acting as a single observatory. It also underscores the high acceptance and exposure of Askaryan detector arrays to ultrahigh energy neutrinos.

cross.summary: The Askaryan Radio Array (ARA) is an in-ice radio observatory at the South Pole designed to detect ultrahigh energy (UHE) neutrinos through Askaryan emission produced by interactions of neutrinos and their secondary particles. In this paper, we present the detailed methodology of the first array-wide search for a diffuse UHE neutrino flux using data from all five ARA stations. The dataset considered represents $10.6$ years of livetime and is three times larger than previous ARA neutrino searches. This search achieves a $28\%$ analysis efficiency for a neutrino flux corresponding to the current experimental upper limits. No neutrino candidates are observed on an expected background of $0.13\pm0.01\text{ (stat.)}^{+0.05}_{-0.06}\text{ (syst.)}$ events. We set a new upper limit on the diffuse UHE neutrino flux, which is the most stringent from $50$ EeV to $1000$ EeV. We also discuss lessons learned for future searches on large radio arrays.

repl.title: Validation of the DESI DR2 Ly$α$ BAO analysis using synthetic datasets
repl.summary: The second data release (DR2) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), containing data from the first three years of observations, doubles the number of Lyman-$\alpha$ (Ly$\alpha$) forest spectra in DR1 and it provides the largest dataset of its kind. To ensure a robust validation of the Baryonic Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) analysis using Ly$\alpha$ forests, we have made significant updates compared to DR1 to both the mocks and the analysis framework used in the validation. In particular, we present CoLoRe-QL, a new set of Ly$\alpha$ mocks that use a quasi-linear input power spectrum to incorporate the non-linear broadening of the BAO peak. We have also increased the number of realisations used in the validation to 400, compared to the 150 realisations used in DR1. Finally, we present a detailed study of the impact of quasar redshift errors on the BAO measurement, and we compare different strategies to mask Damped Lyman-$\alpha$ Absorbers (DLAs) in our spectra. The BAO measurement from the Ly$\alpha$ dataset of DESI DR2 is presented in a companion publication.

repl.title: The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) Antarctic Balloon Payload
repl.summary: The General Antiparticle Spectrometer (GAPS) is an Antarctic stratospheric balloon mission designed to provide unmatched sensitivity to low-energy (< 0.25 GeV/n) cosmic-ray antiprotons, antideuterons, and antihelium nuclei as signatures of dark matter. The distinctive GAPS particle identification technique relies on measuring the energy loss along the track of an incoming antinucleus as it slows down and is captured into an exotic atom, and then detecting the de-excitation X-rays and the nuclear annihilation products. This measurement is realized using a Tracker composed of more than 1000 custom silicon strip detectors and a plastic scintillator time-of-flight (TOF) system instrumenting more than 40 m$^2$. Together, these subsystems provide the velocity and energy resolution, stopping power, particle tracking, and X-ray identification necessary to distinguish rare antinucleus signals from the abundant positive-nucleus backgrounds, all within the constraints of a high-altitude mission. A multi-loop capillary heat pipe system has been developed to maintain the tracker operating temperature with significant mass and power savings over a conventional pump-based system. The first GAPS science payload flew for 25 days during the 2025/26 NASA Antarctic balloon campaign. We detail the design, integration, and commissioning of the payload prior to flight.

repl.title: Carruthers Data Processing Pipeline: Instrument Effect Correction
repl.summary: The Carruthers Geocorona Observatory -- launched in September 2025 -- is NASA's first mission devoted to investigating the fundamental nature of Earth's exosphere from its distant vantage in halo orbit around the Earth-Sun L1 Lagrange point. Its primary payload, the GeoCoronal Imager, consists of two coaligned photometric imagers that measure ultraviolet Lyman-alpha emission radiance from exospheric hydrogen simultaneously at wide- and narrow- fields of view. The imagers use MicroChannel Plate intensified Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor detectors, which are known to add various artifacts to the final image telemetered from the spacecraft, hereby known as instrument effects. This paper details the algorithms used to retrieve and remove instrument effects from raw telemetry on-orbit, including detector voltage bias, thermal dark current, particle radiation, flat-field, and distortion. Finally, the science data processing pipeline from raw telemetry to instrument-effect corrected images is detailed. Algorithm performance is measured via a synthetic numerical image generator or validated on pre-launch experiments.

repl.title: Identifying narrow-band mutual coupling resonances in SKA-low stations using frequency-independent current basis functions
repl.summary: Mutual coupling between closely spaced elements in aperture arrays introduces narrow-band spectral features in the Embedded Element Patterns (EEPs), threatening measurements of the 21-cm power spectrum with instruments such as SKA-low. We detail a method to identify such features through the construction of frequency-independent current basis functions, utilising a singular value decomposition of frequency-dependent basis functions. We demonstrate the method on a three-element linear array and full pseudo-random station of SKA log-periodic antennas and examine the current power induced by mutual coupling. For the pseudo-random layout station we note many narrow-band resonance features, including strong resonances at 50.8~MHz and 83.6~MHz, where the coupled power on the passive antennas can approach or exceed that of the excited antenna. Simulated delay power spectra for the SKA-low core show that observing in frequency bands including resonance features causes large foreground leakage within the delay power spectra, obscuring the EoR window. For the pseudo-random layout station with SKALA4.0 we identify two significant frequency bands from 59.2--76.2~MHz and 84.2--103.3~MHz which are free of contamination from current resonances, preserving the EoR window in these frequency ranges.

repl.title: Science Prospects for the Southern Wide-field Gamma-ray Observatory: SWGO
repl.summary: Ground-based gamma-ray astronomy is now well established as a key observational approach to address critical topics at the frontiers of astroparticle physics and high-energy astrophysics. Whilst the field of TeV astronomy was once dominated by arrays of atmospheric Cherenkov Telescopes, ground-level particle detection has now been demonstrated to be an equally viable and strongly complementary approach. Ground-level particle detection provides continuous monitoring of the overhead sky, critical for the mapping of extended structures and capturing transient phenomena. As demonstrated by HAWC and LHAASO, the technique provides the best available sensitivity above a few tens of TeV, and for the first time access to the PeV energy range. Despite the success of this approach, there is so far no major ground-level particle-based observatory with access to the Southern sky. HESS, located in Namibia, is the only major gamma-ray instrument in the Southern Hemisphere, and has shown the extraordinary richness of the inner galaxy in the TeV band, but is limited in terms of field of view and energy reach. SWGO is an international effort to construct the first wide-field instrument in the south with deep sensitivity from 100s of GeV into the PeV domain. The project is now close to the end of its development phase and planning for construction of the array in Chile has begun. Here we describe the baseline design, expected sensitivity and resolution, and describe in detail the main scientific topics that will be addressed by this new facility and its initial phase SWGO-A. We show that SWGO will have a transformational impact on a wide range of topics from cosmic-ray acceleration and transport to the nature of dark matter. SWGO represents a key piece of infrastructure for multi-messenger astronomy in the next decade, with strong scientific synergies with the nearby CTA Observatory.

repl.title: Modeling Globular Cluster Stellar Streams with a Basis-Expansion N-body Code
repl.summary: Globular cluster stellar streams probe galaxy-formation processes and can potentially reveal the distribution of dark matter in galaxies. In many theoretical studies, streams are modeled with particle-spray or direct N-body codes. But particle-spray methods abstract away the internal dynamics of the progenitor by making strong assumptions about the escape physics, while direct N-body is prohibitively expensive for realistic (N>10^5) systems. In this paper, we present the stream-modeling capabilities of KRIOS, a new basis-expansion N-body code for collisional stellar dynamics, that bridges this runtime vs. accuracy gap. We show that KRIOS reproduces NBODY6++GPU cluster models, and their associated streams, more accurately than particle spray in a fraction of the NBODY6++GPU wall-clock time. We then compare KRIOS to various particle-spray methods on 10 orbits similar to known Milky Way streams. The morphology and kinematics of these streams most disagree when the progenitor is tightly bound to the host, as these systems are often subject to stronger tidal forces. Finally, we discuss which elements of the progenitor physics are most important for modeling stellar streams and how these might be incorporated into particle-spray methods.

repl.title: Calibration of CMB Polarisation Using Cross-Experiment Correlations
repl.summary: Parity-violating physics in the Universe can generate correlations between the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) $E$- and $B$-modes, but detecting such signals requires extremely accurate calibration of instruments. We describe a data-driven method to calibrate the relative polarisation angle between CMB experiments using cross-correlations of observations over a common sky region. Unlike standard self-calibration approaches, this method does not assume vanishing isotropic cosmic birefringence or primordial $EB$ correlations when estimating the relative misalignment angle, and therefore preserves sensitivity to parity-violating physics. As a proof of concept, we forecast the performance of this method using the Simons Observatory (SO) Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs) as a calibrated reference. If they can be calibrated to an uncertainty of $0.08^\circ$, as anticipated from the SO wire grid calibration system, we show that the SO Large Aperture Telescope and Planck could be calibrated to uncertainties of $0.10^\circ$ and $0.17^\circ$, respectively, at $\sim 145$ GHz. This approach relies on the availability of at least one well-calibrated instrument, and provides a complementary path to improving polarisation calibration across experiments, enabling more robust searches for parity-violating physics in the CMB, such as cosmic birefringence.

repl.title: Season by season causal analysis of the continuum and velocity-resolved H$β$ emission of NGC 5548
repl.summary: We investigate possible causal influences in five historical seasons (1989-1993) of NGC 5548 using a version of the Synergistic-Unique-Redundant Decomposition (SURD) method adapted for this analysis, an information-theoretic causal discovery method for time series. Two four-variable sets contain the blue wing (B), core (C) and red wing (R) of H-beta together with either total H-beta (H) or the 5100 Angstrom continuum (F). We examine 7200 decompositions with common and unequal lags, two or three seasonal flux states, and base delays of 1-30 d. We rank the individual named components within each information family, reporting their amplitudes and simultaneous leakage. In 1989, unique continuum information about the core reaches 0.799 and 0.387 of target entropy for two and three states, with leakage 0.047 and 0.276. In 1992, the red-wing history supplies unique information about the future blue wing in both variable sets and both state counts, with peak target-entropy fractions 0.106-0.166. Distinct joint influences also emerge: for the 1991 core, the two-state S(F,B) and S(F,R) components contribute 0.187 and 0.125 at 20 d with leakage 0.087, although the unique continuum term vanishes. Strong core-wing redundancy identifies candidate inputs for simpler predictive models. Large late-lag leakage, reaching approximately 0.97 in the total set, identifies targets for additional driver measurements and richer temporal histories. The resulting seasonal map of individual, shared and joint influences complements the response delays and velocity structure measured by reverberation mapping, and provides specific causal hypotheses for the evolving broad-line region.
